items.stem: Which of the following is an example of coding field notes?
options: Copying notes into a neat notebook
Counting the words in the notes
Deleting notes that seem boring
Labelling every instance of people saving seats as "claiming space"
items.answer: Labelling every instance of people saving seats as "claiming space"
items.markingKey: D. Coding groups data into themes.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an emic category and an analytical concept.
items.answer: An emic category is participants' own term (e.g. "regulars"); an analytical concept is the anthropologist's tool (e.g. belonging, habitus). Good analysis connects the two.
items.markingKey: An emic category is participants' own term (e.g. "regulars"); an analytical concept is the anthropologist's tool (e.g. belonging, habitus). Good analysis connects the two. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why triangulation improves the credibility of fieldwork findings.
items.answer: If observations, interviews and different times point to the same pattern, the interpretation is less likely to reflect a single unusual event or the researcher's bias.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If observations, interviews and different times point to the same pattern, the interpretation is less likely to reflect a single unusual event or the researcher's bias. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

Coded field notes from a student IA at a skate park: "[CLAIMING SPACE] 16.10 Older skaters leave bags on the top of the ramp. [RESPECT] 16.25 A younger boy waits until an older skater nods before dropping in. [CLAIMING SPACE] 16.40 Two girls set up cones on the flat area; older skaters skate around them. [RESPECT?] 16.55 The same girls are asked to move by a man with a scooter; they refuse." The student writes: "Theme: hierarchy based on age."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): coded IA field notes written for this question bank.

Identify and describe how the student coded the observations. Refer closely to the text. Write in your own words and keep close to the evidence in the extract.
items.answer: The student coded bags left on the ramp and the girls' cones as "claiming space"; the boy waiting for a nod as "respect"; the girls' refusal to move with a question mark; and concluded a theme of age-based hierarchy.
items.markingKey: The student coded bags left on the ramp and the girls' cones as "claiming space"; the boy waiting for a nod as "respect"; the girls' refusal to move with a question mark; and concluded a theme of age-based hierarchy. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

Analyse how well the coding supports the student's theme of age-based hierarchy. Support your answer with evidence from the text. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: Several observations support age hierarchy (older skaters' bags on the ramp, the younger boy waiting for a nod), but the girls' cones and refusal to move suggest gender and type of activity also shape claims to space; the question mark shows awareness of a contradictory case that should refine the theme (e.g. hierarchy based on age, gender and skill).

items.stem: "Analysis means repeating what happened in more detail." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Analysis interprets patterns and meanings using concepts; it goes beyond description.
items.markingKey: Analysis interprets patterns and meanings using concepts; it goes beyond description. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

With reference to the text and to professional guidelines such as the AAA Principles of Professional Responsibility, discuss the ethical responsibilities of the anthropologist. Consider the obligations owed to different people involved in the research.
items.answer: Skate parks involve minors; observation should not identify individuals, photographs should be avoided and parental consent sought for any interviews with under-18s. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Skate parks involve minors; observation should not identify individuals, photographs should be avoided and parental consent sought for any interviews with under-18s. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people. Markbands – 9–10: insightful, balanced discussion of ethical dilemmas, competing obligations and possible responses, fully grounded in the text and professional codes; 7–8: well-developed discussion of several ethical issues and competing obligations, closely linked to the text; 5–6: relevant ethical issues explained with reference to the text and to professional principles; 3–4: some relevant ethical issues (e.g. consent, harm) identified and partly explained with reference to the text; 1–2: ethical issues identified only in general terms, with little reference to the text; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that a student IA should use theory from well-known anthropologists rather than develop its own interpretations. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Students should use theory as a tool while letting the data shape their interpretation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: theory shows knowledge and links to the course; it supports analysis; forcing data into theory distorts it; original interpretation from data shows insight. Suitable ethnographies include Geertz's "Deep Play", Bourdieu's Outline of a Theory of Practice, Scott's Weapons of the Weak. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Students should use theory as a tool while letting the data shape their interpretation. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Explain why linking observations to concepts is essential in the IA analysis.
items.answer: Concepts turn description into explanation, show understanding of anthropology and allow the findings to be compared with other ethnographies.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Concepts turn description into explanation, show understanding of anthropology and allow the findings to be compared with other ethnographies. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why emic categories are useful starting points for analysis.
items.answer: Participants' own terms reveal how they classify their world; analysing them avoids imposing outside categories and can lead to deeper interpretation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Participants' own terms reveal how they classify their world; analysing them avoids imposing outside categories and can lead to deeper interpretation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Theory should be chosen before fieldwork and the data made to fit it." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Concepts should help interpret data, and data that do not fit should lead to revision rather than be ignored.
items.markingKey: Concepts should help interpret data, and data that do not fit should lead to revision rather than be ignored. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Geertz's "Deep Play" (in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)) as your example, describe how power is shown.
items.answer: In "deep" matches between high-status men the money matters less than the status symbolically at stake, so the cockfight dramatises the village status hierarchy without actually changing it.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: In "deep" matches between high-status men the money matters less than the status symbolically at stake, so the cockfight dramatises the village status hierarchy without actually changing it. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Clifford Geertz, "Deep Play: Notes on the Balinese Cockfight" (1972; reprinted in The Interpretation of Cultures, 1973), in a Balinese village (fieldwork with Hildred Geertz, 1958)); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

With reference to space, place and time, compare and contrast the text with one ethnography you have studied. You might choose Low's On the Plaza. Refer to specific evidence from both the text and the ethnography.
items.answer: Text: Several observations support age hierarchy (older skaters' bags on the ramp, the younger boy waiting for a nod), but the girls' cones and refusal to move suggest gender and type of activity also shape claims to space; the question mark shows awareness of a contradictory case that should refine the theme (e.g. hierarchy based on age, gender and skill). Ethnography – Setha Low, On the Plaza: The Politics of Public Space and Culture (2000), on two plazas in San José, Costa Rica: Low shows that public space is both socially produced (by history, politics and design) and socially constructed (given meaning through everyday use). Comparison: similarities and differences in how space, place and time is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Compare and contrast how power is shown in Setha Low, On the Plaza: The Politics of Public Space and Culture (2000) and Pierre Bourdieu, Outline of a Theory of Practice (1972; English 1977).
items.answer: Low's On the Plaza (on two plazas in San José, Costa Rica): The municipality's redesign of the Parque Central sparked conflict, as marginal users such as shoeshiners and pensioners were displaced or regulated. Bourdieu's Outline of a Theory of Practice (based on fieldwork among the Kabyle of Algeria (1950s–1960s)): Bourdieu showed how domination is reproduced through habitus – embodied dispositions that make inequality feel natural (doxa) – and through symbolic capital such as honour. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Low's On the Plaza (on two plazas in San José, Costa Rica): The municipality's redesign of the Parque Central sparked conflict, as marginal users such as shoeshiners and pensioners were displaced or regulated. Bourdieu's Outline of a Theory of Practice (based on fieldwork among the Kabyle of Algeria (1950s–1960s)): Bourdieu showed how domination is reproduced through habitus – embodied dispositions that make inequality feel natural (doxa) – and through symbolic capital such as honour. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "evaluation (of fieldwork)"?
options: A recurring pattern or idea identified across the data, such as "claiming space" or "showing respect"
Comparing evidence from different methods, times or participants to check the reliability of an interpretation
Changes in participants' behaviour caused by the presence of the observer
Assessing the strengths and limitations of the methods, data and interpretations in the report
items.answer: Assessing the strengths and limitations of the methods, data and interpretations in the report
items.markingKey: D. "evaluation (of fieldwork)" is assessing the strengths and limitations of the methods, data and interpretations in the report.

items.stem: A student claims: "Description and analysis should be kept in separate parts of the report with no connection." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They should be integrated so that analytical claims are supported by specific descriptive evidence.
items.markingKey: They should be integrated so that analytical claims are supported by specific descriptive evidence. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between limitations of method and limitations of interpretation.
items.answer: Limitations of method concern how data were collected (time, access, sample); limitations of interpretation concern how far conclusions follow from the data and alternative explanations.
items.markingKey: Limitations of method concern how data were collected (time, access, sample); limitations of interpretation concern how far conclusions follow from the data and alternative explanations. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

Paragraph from a student's fieldwork report: "Over four visits to the barber shop, I observed that the same three men sat on the bench by the window each time and joined conversations without being asked (field notes, visits 1–4). Newer customers waited near the door and spoke mainly to the barber. This suggests that the bench is a marker of belonging, similar to how Low found different groups claiming parts of a plaza. However, I only visited on Saturday mornings, so I cannot say whether this pattern holds at other times."

items.stem: Briefly describe Malinowski's detailed ethnographic description and explain what it reveals about integrating description and analysis.
items.answer: Malinowski's account of the kula combined detailed narrative of voyages with analysis of exchange and obligation. His writing shows how rich description of events supports analytical claims about social relations.

items.answer: Description provides the evidence; analysis explains its significance; moving between them shows how interpretations are grounded in data.

items.stem: Which statement is the best example of critical reflection on positionality?
options: "The research went well."
"As a 17-year-old, I was not taken seriously by older members, so I mainly observed younger people."
"Next time I will bring a better pen."
"I enjoyed the fieldwork."
items.answer: "As a 17-year-old, I was not taken seriously by older members, so I mainly observed younger people."
items.markingKey: B. It explains how the researcher's position shaped data.

items.stem: Distinguish between a mistake and a limitation.
items.answer: A limitation is an inherent constraint of the research design (time, sample); a mistake is an avoidable error in carrying it out (a leading question). Both should be acknowledged and their effects explained.
items.markingKey: A limitation is an inherent constraint of the research design (time, sample); a mistake is an avoidable error in carrying it out (a leading question). items.stem: Explain why ethical reflection belongs alongside methodological reflection.
items.answer: Ethical choices (what not to record, how to protect participants) shape the data available and the interpretations possible, so they are part of evaluating the research.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ethical choices (what not to record, how to protect participants) shape the data available and the interpretations possible, so they are part of evaluating the research. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Compare and contrast how power is shown in Setha Low, On the Plaza: The Politics of Public Space and Culture (2000) and Bronisław Malinowski, Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922).
items.answer: Low's On the Plaza (on two plazas in San José, Costa Rica): The municipality's redesign of the Parque Central sparked conflict, as marginal users such as shoeshiners and pensioners were displaced or regulated. Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific (among the Trobriand Islanders of Papua New Guinea (fieldwork 1915–1918)): Holding famous kula valuables and keeping many partners brings renown; chiefs and successful kula men gain status through generosity, so prestige rather than accumulation underpins influence. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

Markbands – 9–10: sustained, insightful comparison of similarities and differences; ethnography fully contextualised; concepts and theory used critically; 7–8: detailed, accurate ethnographic knowledge; developed comparison of similarities and differences linked to key concepts; 5–6: relevant, contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time); explicit comparison with some analysis of similarities and differences; 3–4: some relevant ethnographic knowledge; mostly descriptive, the text and the ethnography treated separately; 1–2: limited knowledge; comparison implicit or absent; little reference to the text or to an ethnography; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that critical reflection is the most important part of the IA. Support your answer with ethnographic material and anthropological theory.
items.answer: Reflection is vital but depends on the quality of the fieldwork and analysis it evaluates.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: it shows understanding of how anthropological knowledge is produced; it demonstrates ethical awareness; without good data and analysis, reflection has little to evaluate; description and analysis carry much of the weight. Suitable ethnographies include Rosaldo's "Grief and a Headhunter's Rage", Briggs's Never in Anger, Abu-Lughod's Veiled Sentiments. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: Reflection is vital but depends on the quality of the fieldwork and analysis it evaluates. Markbands – 13–15: sharply focused, well-structured argument; detailed, accurate ethnography used critically; sophisticated use of concepts and theory; reasoned, supported conclusion; 10–12: focused, well-structured answer; detailed, contextualised ethnography; clear analysis using concepts and theory; some evaluation of perspectives; 7–9: question understood; relevant ethnography with context; some analysis linked to key concepts, partly descriptive; 4–6: some understanding; ethnographic material relevant but thin or poorly contextualised; limited use of concepts; 1–3: little understanding of the question; generalised or inaccurate ethnographic material; mainly description; 0: does not reach the standard described below.

items.stem: "A student IA should use theory from well-known anthropologists rather than develop its own interpretations." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Students should use theory as a tool while letting the data shape their interpretation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: theory shows knowledge and links to the course; it supports analysis. Arguments against: forcing data into theory distorts it; original interpretation from data shows insight. Supported judgement: Students should use theory as a tool while letting the data shape their interpretation. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.

items.stem: "Description is the most important part of a fieldwork report." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Description is essential but the report is judged mainly on how it is analysed and evaluated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: without detailed description, analysis lacks evidence; rich description conveys the setting to readers. Arguments against: analysis and evaluation show anthropological understanding; description alone is not anthropology. Supported judgement: Description is essential but the report is judged mainly on how it is analysed and evaluated.
